objectives: Distinguish wave types + their dispersion relations.
Reason about tidal forces + harmonic constituents.
Connect storm surge + tsunami physics to design.

slides.title: Surface waves: capillary, gravity, wind, swell
slides.body:
**Surface gravity waves** are oscillations of the air-sea interface restored by gravity (small ripples by surface tension). Classes by wavelength λ:

• **Capillary waves** (λ < 1.7 cm): surface tension-dominated. Restoring force = σ k² (σ = surface tension). c² = σ k / ρ.
• **Short gravity waves** (λ > 1.7 cm): gravity restoration. Deep water (h ≫ λ/2π): c² = g/k = (g λ)/(2π). Phase speed grows with wavelength.
• **Long / shallow waves** (h ≪ λ/2π): non-dispersive. c = √(g h). Independent of wavelength. Tsunami physics.
• **Wind-generated waves**: complex spectrum from wind energy → high-frequency capillary + short gravity, redistributed by nonlinear interactions to longer waves. Significant wave height H_s + peak period T_p characterize sea state.
• **Swell**: long-period waves (T > 8 s) propagating thousands of km from distant storms. Dispersive — long waves arrive first.

**Wave energy**: ∝ H². A 2-m wave has 4× the energy of a 1-m. Storm waves can exceed 30 m (Andrea Storm 2007, Draupner platform 2000, etc.). Rogue waves (>2× H_s) once thought myth, now well-documented.

**Breaking**: when wave steepness H/λ > ~0.14 or depth/H < ~1.28, waves break. Beach breaks: shallow water reduces phase speed → wavelength compresses → steepness grows → breaks.

slides.title: Tides: astronomical forcing + harmonic decomposition
slides.body:
**Tides** are very long ocean waves driven by gravitational pull of Moon + Sun.

• **Tide-raising force**: F_tide ∝ (M_tide-body) / r³ (per unit mass, gradient of gravity field across Earth). Moon's contribution: 2× Sun's despite being 27 million times less massive — because the Moon is much closer.
• **Tidal bulge**: water rises on the Moon-facing side (direct gravity) + the opposite side (centrifugal effect of Earth-Moon system rotation around their common center of mass).
• **Diurnal vs semi-diurnal**: Earth's rotation under the tidal bulge gives semi-diurnal (2/day) tides for most places. Where Earth-Moon geometry interacts with continental geometry: diurnal (1/day) tides (Gulf of Mexico, parts of SE Asia).
• **Spring + Neap tides**: when Moon + Sun align (full/new moon), tidal forces sum → spring tides (larger range, ~20%). When 90° apart (quarter moons): neap tides (smaller, ~70% of spring).
• **Tidal range** varies wildly with coastal geometry: open ocean ~1 m; Mediterranean ~0.3 m; Bay of Fundy ~16 m (resonant amplification, world's largest tides); Inland seas (Baltic, Caspian): negligible.

**Harmonic analysis** (Doodson 1921+): represent tide as sum of constituent harmonics:
  η(t) = ∑ A_i cos(2π t / T_i + φ_i)

Main constituents:
- M2 (principal lunar semi-diurnal, T = 12.42 h): dominates most places
- S2 (principal solar semi-diurnal, T = 12.00 h)
- N2, K2: smaller semi-diurnal
- K1, O1: principal diurnal
- Long-period: Mf (fortnightly), Mm (monthly), MSf (lunisolar synodic)

~140 constituents total tracked operationally. Tide prediction at >99% accuracy globally; mariners + harbor operations rely on it.

slides.title: Storm surge + tsunami physics
slides.body:
**Storm surge**: temporary sea-level rise from hurricane winds + low atmospheric pressure. Mechanisms:
• **Wind setup**: onshore winds drive Ekman transport, pile water against coast. Dominant.
• **Pressure setup**: 1 hPa pressure drop → 1 cm sea-level rise (inverse barometer effect).
• **Coastal geometry**: shallow + concave coasts amplify surge (Gulf Coast, Bay of Bengal).
• **Wave setup**: nearshore wave breaking adds ~10-30% to surge depth.

Damage scaling: rough estimate of major hurricane storm surge ~5-9 m above astronomical tide. Hurricane Katrina 2005: ~8 m surge in Mississippi; flooded New Orleans. Bangladesh Bhola cyclone 1970: ~10 m surge, ~500,000 deaths.

**Tsunami**: long-wavelength waves from undersea earthquake/landslide/volcanic activity. Physics:
• Source: vertical seafloor displacement (~m for M8+, ~10m for M9+ EQ).
• Wavelength λ: 100s of km in open ocean.
• In deep ocean (h ~ 4000 m): c = √(gh) ≈ 200 m/s = 720 km/h (jet airliner). Wave height ~0.5-1 m, hardly noticeable.
• As wave shoals on continental shelf (h decreases): c decreases by √(h_deep/h_shallow); wavelength compresses; height grows by Green's law: H ∝ h^(-1/4). 4000 m → 10 m depth: H grows ~5×.
• Run-up on land: depends on coastal geometry, beach slope, focusing. Can exceed 30 m in narrow bays (Lituya Bay 1958: 524 m local mega-tsunami from landslide).

Major recent: 2004 Indian Ocean (M9.1 Sumatra, ~230K deaths); 2011 Tōhoku Japan (M9.0, ~20K deaths + Fukushima); 2018 Sulawesi (Indonesia, M7.5 + tsunami + liquefaction).

question.question: Compute the phase speed of a swell wave propagating across the Pacific
question.goal: A storm in the South Pacific generates swell with period T = 15 s. How long does this wave take to reach the California coast, ~10,000 km away?

steps.prompt: Wavelength λ in deep water? Use λ = g T² / (2π).

steps.motivation: c = λ / T or c = g T / (2π).
steps.reveal: c = 23.4 m/s ≈ 84 km/h. Faster than most ocean currents.

steps.prompt: BUT energy travels at group velocity c_g = c/2 in deep water. Compute travel time over 10,000 km.
steps.motivation: Group velocity is what matters for energy propagation.
steps.reveal: c_g = 23.4 / 2 ≈ 11.7 m/s. Travel time = 10⁷ m / 11.7 m/s ≈ 8.55 × 10⁵ s = ~9.9 days. Storm energy from Antarctic / Southern Ocean reaches California ~10 days later as long-period swell — exactly what surfers track using buoy spectral data + global wind forecasts.

steps.prompt: Why do longer-period waves arrive first?
steps.reveal: Phase speed c ∝ T in deep water. Longer period → faster propagation. So in a wave spectrum generated by a storm, the longest-period waves arrive first (forerunner swell, T ~ 20+ s), followed by progressively shorter waves over hours-days. Surfers + harbor operators use buoy data + forecast models (WaveWatch III, SWAN, ECMWF) to predict arrival + peak conditions days in advance.

question.question: Classify each wave phenomenon by its primary restoring force + characteristic timescale.

items.label: Wind ripples on a pond (λ ~ 1 mm)
Whitecap chop in 15-knot wind (λ ~ 5-15 m, T ~ 2-3 s)
Sumatra 2004 tsunami (λ ~ 200 km, c ~ 800 km/h in deep ocean)

question.explanation:
Wave classification by restoring force + timescale is the basic taxonomy:
• **Capillary** (λ < 1.7 cm): surface tension dominant. Sub-second period. Localized.
• **Short gravity** (λ ~ m to 100s of m): wind-generated locally + swells from distant storms. Periods 1-25 s. Dispersive in deep water; c ∝ √λ.
• **Tide** (λ ~ 1000s of km, periods 12-24 hr): astronomical forcing. Earth-scale wavelengths; influenced by ocean basin shape + Coriolis.
• **Tsunami** (λ ~ 100s of km, periods 10-60 min): triggered by impulsive forcing (EQ, landslide). Long-wave regime (h ≪ λ/2π); non-dispersive; c = √(gh). Crosses oceans in hours.

Each has different physics + different relevance: capillary affects air-sea gas exchange + light reflection; gravity waves drive coastal sediment transport + design loads; tides drive coastal ecosystems + ports; tsunamis are rare but catastrophic.

question.question: Why does the 2004 Sumatra tsunami spread thousands of km across the Indian Ocean with only ~50-cm amplitude in deep water, then grow to 10-30 m runup at coastlines?
options: In deep ocean (h ~ 4000 m), tsunami wavelength is ~200 km but height only ~50 cm — energy per unit area is modest, wave nearly invisible at surface. As wave shoals onto continental shelf, depth drops 100-1000× → wavelength compresses + wave height grows by Green's law H ∝ h^(-1/4) → +5 to 10× height in 10 m water. Coastal focusing (bays, harbors) can multiply this further. Sumatra: 50 cm offshore → 10-30 m at coast = ~50× amplification via shoaling + focusing.
Tsunami waves are bigger near the equator.
Tsunamis only happen in shallow water.
question.explanation:
**Tsunami shoaling physics**:

In deep ocean (h ≫ λ/2π → 'shallow-water' wave regime even at 4 km depth because tsunami λ is enormous):
• c = √(g h) (non-dispersive).
• At h = 4000 m: c = 198 m/s = 713 km/h. λ for 30-min period ≈ 360 km.
• Amplitude ~0.5-1 m, hardly noticeable on a calm sea.

As wave moves into shallower water:
• Phase speed drops: c ∝ √h.
• Wavelength compresses: λ ∝ √h (since period T conserved + c = λ/T).
• Wave height grows: H ∝ h^(-1/4) (energy conservation along the ray — Green's law).

Going from 4000 m to 10 m: H ratio = (4000/10)^(1/4) = 400^(1/4) ≈ 4.5×. From 50 cm at 4000 m → ~2.2 m at 10 m depth. Coastal focusing (V-shaped bays, harbors, refraction) can multiply 2-5× further. Total: 50 cm → 10-30 m runup, depending on local geometry.

**Why Indian Ocean basin shape matters**:
- The 2004 Sumatra-Andaman EQ generated a tsunami radiating in all directions.
- Eastern flank: hit Sumatra + Thailand coasts within 15-30 min — short warning.
- Western flank: hit Sri Lanka, India, Maldives ~2 hours later; East Africa ~7 hours later.
- Lack of Indian Ocean tsunami warning system in 2004 meant no alerts even hours after the event. Post-2004: Indian Ocean tsunami warning system (IOTWS) deployed by 2006.

**Tsunami warning today**:
- DART buoys (Deep-ocean Assessment + Reporting of Tsunamis): pressure sensors detect tsunami passage in deep ocean within minutes.
- Computational models (NOAA's SIFT, JMA's NOWPHAS): forecast inundation maps within ~30 min of EQ.
- Coastal sirens, mobile alerts, evacuation plans.
- 2011 Tōhoku (Japan): ~3 min EQ early-warning + ~10 min tsunami alert — but inundation maps underestimated runup; ~20K deaths still occurred.

Design + planning: coastal nuclear plants, infrastructure, communities now plan for 1-in-1000-year tsunami events. Japan's post-Tōhoku coastal walls (~15 m height) are visible monuments to the lesson.

slides.workedSolution: Tsunami in deep ocean: λ ~ 200-360 km, H ~ 0.5-1 m, c ~ 700+ km/h. As wave shoals to coast: c ∝ √h, λ ∝ √h, H ∝ h^(-1/4). From 4000 m to 10 m: H grows ~4.5×; coastal focusing adds further 2-5×. Total: 0.5 m offshore → 10-30 m coastal runup. Indian Ocean 2004: lack of warning system + long propagation times → ~230K deaths. Post-2004: DART buoys + IOTWS + computational forecasts deployed. Modern coastal planning accounts for 1-in-1000-yr events.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why tide prediction at most ports is now accurate to ~5-10 cm, while tsunami prediction remains much more uncertain.
question.rubric: Mentions: tides driven by celestial mechanics (Moon + Sun orbital positions) — fully deterministic + decades of harmonic-constituent analysis at each port. Each port has a calibrated tide-gauge record + 140+ harmonic constants. Predictions for years ahead. Tsunamis: triggered by impulsive seafloor displacement (earthquake, landslide, volcanic). Each event has unique source mechanism, fault geometry, displacement field. Real-time inversion of seismic data + DART buoy measurements + numerical propagation models gives ~minutes-hours warning, but spatially resolved inundation depends on local bathymetry + coastal geometry + nonlinear runup processes. Better than 2004 (no warning system) but still uncertain in detail. Better tools: real-time GNSS, ocean-bottom seismometers, AI-based prediction. Concludes: deterministic forcing (tides) gives precise long-range prediction; impulsive forcing (tsunami) gives uncertain real-time prediction. Different problems, different methods.
